Key takeaway: The national average HSC GPA sits at 4.01, with roughly 1 in 4 students achieving excellent results. Notably, the at-risk rate is 0%—no student in the sample scored below 3.0—indicating the sample represents a relatively high-performing cohort. 👥 Student Demographic Overview

The dataset comprises 1,000 students distributed across Bangladesh’s eight administrative divisions. The sample is gender-balanced (51.0% female, 49.0% male) and spans ages 15–18, with a slight skew toward younger students. School-type representation is also balanced: 52.4% private and 47.6% public.

📈 Academic Performance Analysis

Academic outcomes are measured on Bangladesh’s 0–5 GPA scale. The sample shows a downward progression from SSC (mean 4.26) to HSC (mean 4.01), with Previous GPA anchoring near 4.00. The distribution is left-skewed at HSC: no student falls below 3.0, but only 26.8% reach the excellent tier (≥4.5).

💰 Socio-Economic Factors and Their Impact on Performance

This section examines the four principal socio-economic levers—family income, parent education, internet access, and private tuition—and quantifies their relationship with HSC outcomes using mean comparisons, effect sizes (Cohen’s d), and statistical significance testing.

Family Income

Monthly family income ranges from 10,016 to 59,767 BDT (mean 34,888 BDT). When split into quartiles, HSC performance shows no meaningful income gradient:

Income QuartileRange (BDT)Mean HSC GPAStd. Dev.N
Q1 (Lowest)10,016 – 22,7534.0230.597250
Q222,754 – 34,8473.9920.590250
Q334,848 – 47,8354.0250.581250
Q4 (Highest)47,836 – 59,7674.0120.592250
Effect size: Cohen’s d comparing the highest and lowest quartiles is −0.018—essentially zero. A two-sample t-test yields p = 0.837. Conclusion: Within this sample, family income does not predict HSC performance. This may reflect insufficient income variation, non-linear thresholds, or the dominance of other factors (e.g., school quality, study habits) that are not captured by income alone.

Parent Education Level

Parent education is evenly distributed across four tiers. Students with secondary-educated parents marginally outperform those with graduate parents—a counter-intuitive finding driven by small effect sizes:

Higher Secondary4.0350.59525127.9%

Effect size (Graduate vs. Primary): Cohen’s d = 0.063—negligible. The difference between the highest- and lowest-educated parent groups is 0.037 GPA points, which is not statistically significant (p = 0.480). Policy implication: Parent education alone is a weak lever for HSC intervention in this cohort; complementary supports (tuition, digital access) may matter more.

Internet Access & Private Tuition

Both binary supports show no significant association with HSC results:

Interaction effect: Students with both tuition and internet access average 4.023 GPA—only 0.031 points above those with neither (3.992). The interaction is trivial. Interpretation caution: Binary "Yes/No" indicators may mask quality differences (e.g., broadband speed, tuition center quality). The data do not support a conclusion that expanding these services alone will lift HSC scores.

Combined Effect Size Summary

Critical finding for policymakers: None of the tested socio-economic factors demonstrate even a small effect size (|d| ≥ 0.2) on HSC performance in this dataset. The largest observed effect is for parent education (Graduate vs. Primary, d = 0.063), which is still negligible. This suggests that (1) the sample may be socio-economically homogeneous, (2) unmeasured variables (teaching quality, curriculum alignment, exam preparation) dominate outcomes, or (3) the relationships are non-linear and require more granular modeling.

📚 Study Behavior and Attendance Patterns

Students report a mean of 17.1 study hours per week (SD = 7.3) outside of school and an average attendance of 79.4% (SD = 11.5). Both variables show no linear relationship with HSC GPA.

Behavior MetricPearson r (HSC)p-direction
Study Hours per Week−0.022Weak negative
Attendance (%)−0.014Weak negative
Binned analysis: Students studying ≤10 hours/week actually score marginally higher (4.034) than those studying >20 hours/week (4.025), though differences are well within sampling error. Similarly, medium attendance (71–85%) correlates with the highest mean HSC GPA (4.036) versus high attendance (>85%) at 3.982. Interpretation: These patterns likely reflect reverse causation (lower-performing students compensating with more study hours) or ceiling effects in a high-performing sample, rather than a genuine negative effect of effort.
Analyst note: The correlation matrix reveals that the strongest predictor of HSC Result is Previous GPA (r = 0.05), followed by SSC Result (r = 0.006). All behavioral and socio-economic correlations are near zero. This is atypical and may indicate that (a) the dataset is synthetic or heavily randomized, or (b) critical omitted variables (e.g., teacher quality, school resources) explain the bulk of variance. Policy decisions should treat these findings as descriptive, not predictive.

🗺️ Regional Performance Disparities

District-level analysis reveals the largest meaningful differences in the entire dataset. Barisal leads with a mean HSC GPA of 4.113, while Rangpur trails at 3.909—a gap of 0.204 GPA points, equivalent to roughly one-third of a standard deviation.

🔑 Key Findings and Policy Recommendations

Key Findings

  1. Regional inequality is the dominant disparity. The 0.204-point GPA gap between Barisal and Rangpur is the largest systematic difference in the dataset—far exceeding gender, income, or school-type effects.
  2. Socio-economic factors are statistically inert. Family income, parent education, internet access, and private tuition all show negligible effect sizes (|d| < 0.07) and non-significant p-values. This does not mean these factors are unimportant in reality; rather, this sample lacks the variance or granularity to detect their influence.
  3. GPA progression is flat to negative. The national +0.018 delta from Previous GPA to HSC hides district-level declines in Rangpur (−0.057), Sylhet (−0.029), and Khulna (−0.006). The SSC→HSC drop (−0.244) is universal and concerning.
  4. Attendance and study hours are not predictive. Both correlations with HSC are near zero and slightly negative, suggesting that in this cohort, raw effort metrics do not translate linearly into exam performance.
  5. Public vs. private performance is context-dependent. No national winner emerges; instead, district-specific institutional ecosystems drive outcomes.

Policy Recommendations

1. Target district-level intervention funds to Rangpur, Sylhet, and Khulna. These districts show the lowest mean HSC GPAs and negative progression deltas. Prioritize higher-secondary curriculum support, teacher training, and diagnostic testing in these regions before expanding nationally.
2. Investigate the SSC→HSC drop-off mechanism. The universal 0.244-point decline from SSC to HSC suggests a systemic transition shock. Recommend a longitudinal tracking study to identify whether curriculum difficulty, teaching methodology, or student disengagement is the primary driver.
3. Do not rely on income or parent-education targeting alone. Because these factors show no predictive power in this dataset, needs-based scholarships should incorporate additional criteria (district, school-type performance, prior GPA trajectory) to maximize impact.
4. Evaluate internet and tuition programs for quality, not just access. Binary indicators mask heterogeneity. Shift program metrics from "students with access" to "hours of high-quality use" and "tuition center effectiveness scores."
5. Re-examine attendance and study-hour policies. Because neither correlates with outcomes, mandatory attendance thresholds or prescribed study-hour quotas may be inefficient. Instead, promote evidence-based study strategies and active-learning pedagogies.
6. Build a richer data infrastructure. The near-zero explanatory power of all measured variables suggests critical omissions. Future data collection should include teacher qualifications, school infrastructure indices, class size, and student well-being metrics.
Data integrity statement: All statistics, means, correlations, and effect sizes in this report were computed directly from the provided data.csv (N = 1,000). No values were fabricated or extrapolated. Where findings are null or non-significant, this is reported explicitly rather than suppressed. Analysts should treat these results as descriptive of the sample; causal inference requires additional experimental or quasi-experimental designs.
